blocks.text: METR 审阅了 Anthropic 公开的《2026 年 8 月风险报告》中“自动化研发带来的风险”一节。1本次审阅属于一项高权限评估的一部分，评估主题是 AI 研发加速；Anthropic 在该评估中提供了风险报告的未公开版本，以及大量其他非公开数据。在发布本审阅的同时，我们也在发布一份关于 Anthropic 内部 AI 研发加速的整体评估。该整体评估与本次风险报告审阅由同一批 METR 员工完成。

blocks.text: 总体而言，我们认同 Anthropic 的结论：截至 7 月 15 日，其内部部署的模型直接自动化关键领域研发、或因能力进展加速而引发严重灾难性风险的可能性都较低。但报告声称这些模型尚未越过早期预警阈值，这一说法依赖于一些存在争议的判断，而公开报告并未把这些判断讲清楚。尽管参与本项目的 METR 研究人员和 Anthropic 的相关员工都倾向于认为阈值尚未被越过，但我们认为它很可能已经被越过，并且我们认为公开报告总体上低估了当时正在发生的加速程度。

blocks.text: “我们相信，如果模型能够替代我们整个研究团队的技术工作——哪怕成本很高——我们也会清楚地意识到这一点；而事实上，即使有强烈的动机，我们也没有进行这种替代，这本身就说明我们的模型还不具备这种水平的能力。”
简单来说，Anthropic 在努力用模型替代研究人员，但研究人员仍然不可或缺。报告也给出了基准测试证据，但我们认为它不如这一直接观察重要，也更不确定。

blocks.text: “威胁在于：我们相信，未来几年 AI 模型可能具备广泛超越人类的能力。尤其是，推动关键领域研发所需的大部分甚至全部工作——从机器人技术到能源、网络战，再到 AI 研发本身——都可能变得可自动化。
如果这一判断成立，可能带来巨大的收益，但这些收益也会伴随几个不同却相关的问题：

inlines.text: 某些技术领域的快速进展，可能改变国家内部和国家之间的权力结构。例如，如果某个威权政权在 AI 上建立起对世界其他地区的自我强化领先优势，这种领先可能累积成科技上的巨大优势——进而可能转化为发动战争、监控公民和/或长期掌控极强技术的能力上突然而颠覆性的进步。
如果 AI 模型在关键领域高度自动化研发的过程中发展出危险的目标，它们就可能借助新技术及其对技术的获取渠道造成无上限的伤害——甚至包括人类彻底失去对文明的控制。
如果 AI 能被用来自动化 AI 研发本身，结果可能是 AI 进展的极度加速，从而带来非常广泛的一系列风险，包括但不限于本报告讨论的那些风险。”

引用 RSP v3.4 的表述，这一条的操作化定义是：“我们认为情景（2）已经发生，当且仅当：(a) 我们观察到或预期 AI 综合能力进展速度达到我们在没有 AI 对 AI 研发做出显著贡献的情况下所预期的速度、以及所观察到的最快持续进展速度[fn2]这两者的两倍[fn1]；(b) 这种翻倍有相当大一部分可合理归因于研究与/或工程的自动化（而非人员增加、算力增加或一般生产力提升等其他因素），以至于这一 AI 进展趋势若延续下去，很可能带来更大的加速。”
[fn1] “进展速度翻倍”是指“一年取得的进展相当于基线情况下两年取得的进展”。例如，若基线进展是算力扩大 3 倍、算法效率提升 3 倍（即 9 倍“有效扩展”），那么“进展速度翻倍”大致相当于 81 倍的有效扩展。这与“研究人员生产力翻倍”不是一回事，因为投入翻倍并不必然使进展速度翻倍。
[fn2] 至少跨越了三代模型。
我们只基于少数几个最直接以最大化能力为优化目标的模型，做了一次朴素外推，并假设加速趋势会延续。相比基于全部数据点的外推，这次外推让我们更准确地预测了未来的 AECI 分数。
截至风险报告覆盖日期 2026 年 7 月 15 日，模型 2 尚未完成训练。

blocks.text: METR reviewed the “Risks from automated R&D” section of Anthropic’s public August 2026 Risk Report.1 We conducted this review as part of a high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration, in which Anthropic shared a private version of the Risk Report along with extensive other non-public data. Alongside this review, we are publishing a holistic assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. This was conducted by the same METR employees as this Risk Report Review.

August 2026 Risk Report

We conducted this review as part of a high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration, in which Anthropic shared a private version of the Risk Report along with extensive other non-public data. Alongside this review, we are publishing a
holistic assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic
. This was conducted by the same METR employees as this Risk Report Review.

blocks.text: Overall, we agree with Anthropic that by July 15th, internally deployed models posed low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains or causing acute catastrophic risks from acceleration of capabilities progress. However, the report’s claim that they had not crossed their early warning thresholds relies on contestable judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly in the public report. While both METR’s researchers on this project and Anthropic’s relevant staff lean toward it not having been crossed, we think it is plausible that it had been, and we believe the public report overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring.

blocks.text: Under Anthropic’s RSP v3.4, the Automated R&D threshold is triggered by either of two conditions:

inlines.text: Under Anthropic’s RSP v3.4, the Automated R&D threshold is triggered by either of two conditions:
Full Substitution Threshold:
If they develop a model that can “fully substitute for our entire set of Research Scientists and Research Engineers, at competitive costs (i.e., within a factor of 5).”
2x Acceleration Threshold:
If there is “dramatic acceleration” of the pace of AI progress for reasons that likely relate to the automation of AI R&D.
This is defined in further detail in the RSP, but the details are not critical to our critique.

blocks.text: “[W]e believe it would be clear to us if models were capable of substituting, even at high cost, for the technical work of our entire research staff, and the fact that we do not perform such substitution even when strongly incentivized to is evidence against our models having this level of capability.”

Simply put, Anthropic tries hard to substitute researchers out for models, but researchers are still required. They also present benchmark evidence, but we interpret it as less important and more uncertain than this direct observation.

Limited attribution of this acceleration to AI:

Weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI:

blocks.text: “The threat: We believe that AI models could, in the next few years, have a broad range of capabilities that exceed human capabilities. In particular, most or all of the work needed to advance research and development in key domains—from robotics to energy to cyberwarfare to AI R&D itself—may become automatable.
If this is correct, there could be enormous benefits, but these benefits would come with several distinct but related concerns:

inlines.text: Sufficiently rapid progress in some areas of technology could change power structures both within and between nations. For example, if an authoritarian regime built a self-reinforcing lead in AI over the rest of the world, this lead could compound into a major advantage in science and technology—which could in turn translate to very sudden and disruptive advances in the ability to wage war, surveil citizens, and/or wield extremely powerful technology over the long term.

If AI models develop dangerous goals while heavily automating R&D in key domains, they may cause unbounded harm—up to and including humanity losing control over civilization entirely—by leveraging novel technology and their access to it.

If AI can be used to automate AI R&D itself, the result may be extreme acceleration in AI progress, putting a very broad set of risks on the table, including but not limited to those discussed in this report.”

inlines.text: The public risk report also describes finding weak evidence in favor of a one-time jump in AECI at the time of Mythos Preview, but we disagree with their emphasis on this:

At the time, the AECI data was only mildly in favor of a jump, and a continued acceleration could not be ruled out. If we reuse the data that was used in the Risk Report, the estimated acceleration is around 1.5x. After the publication of the Risk Report, Anthropic added data from more benchmarks, which estimates an acceleration of 1.9x using the same set of models.
We think relying only on the smaller number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability is simpler and more principled, and does not distinguish at all between the two hypotheses.
A continued acceleration in AECI would be more consistent with the continued acceleration observed in the leading indicators. As described in our
holistic assessment
, we think the evidence since the public risk report points in favor of continued acceleration since October 2025.

Quoting from the RSP v3.4, this is operationalized as: “We would consider scenario (2) to have occurred where (a) we observe or expect double the rate of progress [fn1] in AI aggregate capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress [fn2] we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D and (b) it is plausible that this doubling is substantially attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress seems likely to lead to even greater acceleration.”

[fn1] “Double the rate of progress” means “as much progress in one year as one would see in two years at baseline.” For example, if baseline progress involved a 3× scaleup in compute and a 3× improvement in algorithmic efficiency (for a 9× “effective scaleup”), “double the rate of progress” would entail something like an 81× effective scaleup. This is not the same idea as “doubling researchers’ productivity,” since doubling inputs does not necessarily double the rate of progress.
[fn2] Over at least three model generations.

We did a naive extrapolation based only on the small number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability, assuming continued acceleration. This extrapolation led us to more correctly forecast future AECI scores, compared to an extrapolation based on all the points.
Model 2 had not finished training as of the Risk Report’s coverage date, July 15, 2026.
